newsitem.title: JAPAN: US urges Japan to stick to insurance deregulation.
newsitem.headline: US urges Japan to stick to insurance deregulation.

text.p: The United States urged Japan on Wednesday to maintain momentum in deregulating its insurance sector, calling for faster product approval and greater transparency in the industry.

Japan had made some progress but foreign market share in insurance remained the lowest of the G7 countries at 3.9 percent, a U.S. official told reporters after the two sides held follow-up talks to an insurance pact made in December.
The official said it was still taking too much time for new products to get to the market and that the Finance Ministry needed to employ more personnel and make the approval process more transparent.

Under heavy pressure from Washington, Japan agreed last year to loosen rules in so-called primary sector insurance -- mainly life, car, fire and casualty insurance -- with most of the focus on the tightly-controlled non-life sector.
But the pact upset domestic insurers and analysts said they were likely to fight tooth and nail against any further deregulatory efforts while working hard to regain lost ground.

"The industry is vehemently opposed to the agreement. They were deeply shocked that it was signed and are looking for ways to claw back most of what it gave away," said David Threadgold, analyst at BZW Securities Japan.

Media reports that Ministry of Finance committees will not specify an early deadline for banks' entry to the insurance sector in key reports due out this Friday have also reinforced the view that wholesale deregulation is not yet in sight.
But many also argue that the measures already agreed on will bring significant changes to the non-life insurance industry.
"The game-plan has changed," said Paul Heaton, an analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell who added that companies were moving away from being cocooned by assured profits to a more aggressive stance.
He predicts mergers between large and small companies, greater efforts to expand market share and product range, particularly those products aimed at corporate clients.

Under the pact, car insurance sales channels were broadened to allow mail order insurance and credit card payments and from September 1997 insurers will be able to freely set premium rates for car insurance based on a wider range of risk factors.
In addition, the rate setting power of rating organisations will be removed by around mid-1998.

The first foray by a foreign company to take advantage of new measures has been by American Homes, a unit of American International Group, which has started offering mail order car insurance with a 10 percent discount.
The move in early December triggered a selling of shares in the non-life sector.

There has been some rebound but Deutsche Morgan's Heaton believes the non-life insurers, especially the larger firms, are still a good buy, citing conservative reserving policies, strong balance sheets and business expansion prospects.

Analysts say foreign firms are not likely to grab significant market share quickly or engage in a price war with giants such as Tokio Marine & Fire Insurance Co Ltd but say that they could act as a catalyst for lower pricing.

"It's sleeping with an elephant. They have to make certain the thing doesn't roll over on them. They have to run around, chip away, pick up the odd bit of profitable business, making sure they hold onto their existing business and try very hard not to provoke a backlash," said BZW's Threadgold.
